name: e01_bias_waterfall
title: 1. The bias waterfall: how much of +505% was real?
text:
**Question.** How much of the notebook's +505.1% for an EMA50/200 crossover on NVDA (vs +346.6% buy-and-hold, 2022-2024) survives once each backtesting bias is removed?

**Setup.** Step 0 replays the notebook (`legacy_notebook_backtest`); steps 1-4 remove one bias at a time, cumulatively, on the same 03 Jan 2022 to 31 Dec 2024 window, with buy-and-hold under identical settings and Sharpe always in excess of T-bills. Step 5 re-runs the step-4 rule on NVDA's full history, after the README, and on QQQ and SPY.

**Findings.**

- The replica reproduces the README: 505.1% vs 346.6%, from 1 purchase in three years.
- Warm EMAs plus the *state* rule (long while EMA50 > EMA200) is the decisive correction: 281.2% (-223.9 pp). On 03 Jan 2022 the warmed EMA50 was 27% above EMA200, so the rule starts invested and only exits on 29 Apr 2022, after NVDA had fallen 38%. The notebook's EMAs, seeded at the first close, 'death-crossed' on 04 Jan 2022 (a sell while already flat) and first bought on 08 Feb 2023. Seeded EMAs alone (505%) or cross-only entries alone (519%) each keep the rule out of the 2022 crash; only both corrections together give 281%.
- Next-close fills add 31.9 pp. Under step-4 settings same-close, next-open and next-close give 290%, 301% and 322%: with 2 round trips, a handful of fill prices move the result by 33 pp.
- 5 bp/side costs take 0.6 pp; T-bill interest on idle cash *helps* by +9.7 pp (in cash 25% of the time at 3.1% a year).
- Honest result: 322.2% vs 346.3% (-24.2 pp), max drawdown -38.9% vs -62.7%, Sharpe 1.19 vs 1.10 (bootstrap 95% CI of the difference [-0.57, +0.76]).
- Full history (2000-2026, 14 round trips): the rule trails on CAGR, 26.6% vs 30.0%, max drawdown -69% vs -90%, Sharpe 0.74 vs 0.72 (CI [-0.26, +0.33]). After the README: 13.6% vs 56.1%; the rule sold on 08 Apr 2025 and bought back on 22 May 2025 38% higher, with the same -37% drawdown as buy-and-hold.

**Interpretation.** The +505% was an initialisation artefact, not an edge. The backtest opens in cash 35 days after NVDA's Nov 2021 high (10% below it), and seeded EMAs and cross-only entries each keep it there through the 2022 bear market. Corrected, the +158.6 pp lead over buy-and-hold becomes a 24.2 pp shortfall. What is left is the drawdown control Faber (2007) documents for moving-average timing, here bought with lower return. Zakamulin (2014) finds that such rules' gains are concentrated in a few long bear markets and depend heavily on the sample, and that is the pattern here: over 2022-2024 it beat buy-and-hold on QQQ (+10.5 pp) and roughly matched it on SPY (-0.3 pp), with shallower drawdowns on both, while on NVDA after the README it trailed buy-and-hold by 42 pp, selling into the short April 2025 sell-off and buying back 38% higher. Neither Sharpe difference is distinguishable from zero (both bootstrap CIs contain it): the evidence for a trend premium (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen 2017) comes from diversified portfolios of dozens of futures markets, which one stock and a few round trips cannot test. Finally, NVDA was picked with hindsight (buy-and-hold CAGR 30% since 2000 vs 9% for SPY): that choice is an unrecorded trial which none of the statistics above account for (Sullivan, Timmermann & White 1999; Bailey & Lopez de Prado 2014).
after: Caveat: Yahoo adjusted prices are not point-in-time (they are rewritten after every split and dividend), so the cached series differs slightly from the one the notebook downloaded; the replica is within 0.04 pp (strategy) and 0.05 pp (buy-and-hold) of the README figures, which are quoted to one decimal.
